To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have measured the membrane viscosity of red cells in two dimensions and that the value we have obtained is in agreement with the predictions from a recent theoretical model.

the transient time upon flow startup of red blood cells confined in microchannels is a function of the imposed flow strength and that such dependence gives access to the effective viscosity and to the elastic modulus controlling their temporal response.

the viscoelastic transient time of red blood cells confined in a microchannel depends on the imposed pressure gradient and can be exploited to estimate the two-dimensional membrane effective viscosity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fundamental physics of the viscoelasticity of red blood cells in confinement.
the viscoelasticity of red blood cells confined in a two-dimensional geometry.
the rheology of the red cell membrane in a two-dimensional confinement, which is of fundamental interest in itself.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 2D viscosity of the red cell membrane is η(mem)(2d) ∼ 5 ⋅ 10(-7)-1.5 ⋅ (10(-6)) N ⋅ m/s, depending on the experimental conditions.
η(mem)(2)D is of the order of 10(-7)-10(-6) N ⋅n ⋅ s⋅m(-1).
the membrane viscosity of red cells is in the range 10(-6) N ⋅n⋅m(-1) < η(mem)(2d) < 10(-5) N ⋊⋅m-1.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the viscoelastic response time upon flow onset of red blood cells is a function of the flow strength, and can be used to determine the effective viscosity and elastic modulus of red cell membranes.

the transient response of red blood cells upon flow startup is a direct consequence of the viscoelastic nature of their membrane, and that the effective viscosity η(mem)(2d) of the membrane can be extracted from such an analysis.

the transient response of a red blood cells flowing through a microchannel is governed by two distinct timescales, which are associated with the viscous dissipation in the cell core, and the elastic response of the membrane.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the membrane viscosity can be accurately determined from the transient response of red blood cells in microfluidic devices.

the transient response of red blood cells to flow can be exploited for a simple and reliable determination of both the elastic modulus and the membrane viscosity, which are key parameters for the characterization of red blood cell membrane mechanics.
the transient time of a confined red blood cell can be used to extract information on its viscoelastic properties, which are crucial for understanding the flow of red blood cells in microcirculation.
